O Indra, we who are praisers call on you alone, praying, for the gain of food. Other men too call on you alone for help, when they are fighting with enemies in battles accompanied by horses, you who are the protector of good men and the best.
We worshippers invoke you for the acquirement of food; you, Indra, the protector of the good, (do) men (invoke for aid) against enemies, and in places where horses (enconnter).

O wonderful (चित्र (*citra*), worthy of admiration) Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt in your hand (vajra-armed), possessor of the thunderbolt, or else, since the thunderbolt is that by which one tears, the possessor of that; such an Indra, bold (धृष्णुया (*dhṛṣṇuyā*), the assailer of enemies) and great: being praised by us, grant us (सं किर (*saṃ kira*), bestow well) the cow and the horse that draws the chariot. As you give abundant food (सत्रा (*satrā*), much) for enjoyment to a man who has conquered (जिग्युषे (*jigyuṣe*)), so do you give: this is the sense.
- वज्रहस्त (*vajrahasta*)—holding the thunderbolt in the hand
- जिग्युषे (*jigyuṣe*)—to a man who is victorious, for enjoyment
- वाजं न (*vājaṃ na*)—as you give food
notes: ಹಿಂಡಿರುವವನೂ printed in the gloss of ಅದ್ರಿವಃ; read as ಹಿಡಿದಿರುವವನೂ "holding"

en: O Indra, wonder-working and holding the thunderbolt in your hand, you who are the assailer of enemies, great-souled and renowned, being praised by us, provide us too with cattle and horses, as you give abundant food to a man who is victorious, for enjoyment.

Wonderful wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra, the lord of clouds, mighty in resolution, being glorified by us. grant us cattle, and horses fit for chariots, as (you grant) abundant food to him who is victorious (in battle).

In the Mahāvrata, in the niṣkevalya, the remainder of the sūkta beginning with यः सत्राहा (*yaḥ satrāhā*) is to be recited. For it is laid down: यः सत्राहा विचर्षणिरिति शेषोऽयं ते अस्तु हर्यत इति सूक्ते । (*yaḥ satrāhā vicarṣaṇiriti śeṣo 'yaṃ te astu haryata iti sūkte |*) (Ai. Ā. 5-2-4) **GLOSS** On the Cāturviṃśika day, at the midday pressing, the pragātha यः सत्राहेति (*yaḥ satrāheti*) is an optional anurūpa. And it is laid down in the sūtra: यः सत्राहा विचर्षणः स्वादोरित्था विषूवतः । (*yaḥ satrāhā vicarṣaṇaḥ svādoritthā viṣūvataḥ |*) (Ā. 7-4) **GLOSS** ⟨NOTE:60⟩ The Indra who is the slayer (सत्राहा (*satrāhā*)) of mighty enemies and the all-seer (विचर्षणिः (*vicarṣaṇiḥ*), he who sees everything in particular): that Indra we call (हूमहे (*hūmahe*)), summoning him with words of praise. The latter half is in the direct address. O thousand-organed one (सहस्रमुष्क (*sahasramuṣka*), with a thousand members), whatever woman Indra met, in his eagerness for enjoyment

he sent forth organs in his own body, at every joint: so the Kauṣītakins have handed down. With this in mind the address is made. O you of much wealth (तुविनृम्म (*tuvinṛmma*)), O protector of the good (सत्पते (*satpate*)), Indra, be in battles (समत्सु (*samatsu*)) for our increase (वृधे (*vṛdhe*)).
notes: the bhāṣya cites the pragātha ಯಃ ಸತ್ರಾಹಾ with the reference ಆ. ೭-೪; the Kannada ವಿಶೇಷವಿಷಯಗಳು after this Ṛk speaks of ಇಂದ್ರ ಜ್ಯೇಷ್ಠಂ ನ ಆ ಭರ with the same reference

en: - सहस्रमुष्क (*sahasramuṣka*)—O you who have thousands of organs of enjoyment
- तुविनृम्म (*tuvinṛmma*)—who have many kinds of wealth
- सत्पते (*satpate*)—and are the protector of good men, O Indra

The Indra who is the destroyer of enemies and is able to see everything, that same Indra we call, praying. O Indra, who have thousands of organs of enjoyment, who have many kinds of wealth and are the protector of good men, be the increaser for us in battles.

We invoke that Indra who is the destroyer of mighty foes, the supervisor (of all things): you, the many-organed, the protector to the good, the distributor of wealth, be unto us (the ensurer of) successs in combats.

On the day of the sacrifice called Cāturviṃśaka, at the time of the midday pressing, the priest called Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin may recite, optionally, for the anurūpa Ṛk, the Ṛk (pragātha) इंद्र ज्येष्ठं न आ भर (*iṃdra jyeṣṭhaṃ na ā bhara*); this is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta-sūtra, इंद्र ज्येष्ठं न आ भरा त्वा सहस्रमा शतं (*iṃdra jyeṣṭhaṃ na ā bharā tvā sahasramā śataṃ*) (Ā. 7-4).

O ऋचीषम (*ṛcīṣama*), one who is like the Ṛk, that is, whose form is such as the Ṛk sets forth: such an Indra, in battle (माळ्वे (*māḷve*)), the crusher and harasser of enemies (घृषौ (*ghṛṣau*)), you assail (बाधसे (*bādhase*), assail!) the people, our enemies, with strong anger (मन्युना (*manyunā*)), as a bull would. And in the battle that is the cause of great wealth, be our protector (अविता (*avitā*)); बोधि (*bodhi*) means know yourself as protector, that is, be our protector. For what purpose? For the gain of those things that are to be obtained, among them the offspring (तनूषु (*tanūṣu*)), the waters, and the sun (सूर्ये (*sūrye*)); the gain of the sun is its sight; for that, is the meaning. ⟨NOTE:61⟩
notes: ಫೃಷೌ in the Saṃhitā and Pratipadārtha, ಘೃಷೌ in the bhāṣya; ಮೀಳ್ಹ in the Saṃhitā, ಮಾಳ್ಹೀ in the Pada, ಮಾಳ್ವೇ in the bhāṣya; the bhāṣya words ತನಯೇಷ್ಟಪ್ಪೂಡಕೇಷು are damaged and the sentence is read here as "offspring, waters"

en: - ऋचेषम (*ṛceṣama*)—O Indra, whose form is set forth by the Ṛk and the other mantras
- महाधने (*mahādhane*)—in the battle which is the cause of abundant wealth
- अविता (*avitā*)—that you should be the protector
- तनूषु (*tanūṣu*)—for the gain of sons and the rest
- अप्पु (*appu*)—and for the gain of water
- सूर्ये (*sūrye*)—and for our obtaining the light of the sun (be our protector)

O Indra, whose form is set forth by the Ṛk and the other mantras, in the battle fought with enemies destroy the enemy people with anger as powerful as a bull's. Know that you should be our protector in the battle that is the cause of abundant wealth. And be our protector for the gain of sons and the rest for us, for the gain of water, and for our obtaining the light of the sun.

Such, Indra, as you are represented in holy texts, assail (our) adversaries with fierceness like (that of) a bull in close conflict: regard yourself as our defender in war, (that we may long enjoy) posterity, water, and the (sight of the) sun.

On the Cāturviṃśika day, at the midday pressing, the pragātha of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, इंद्र ज्येष्ठं न आ भरेति (*iṃdra jyeṣṭhaṃ na ā bhareti*), is an optional anurūpa; this is laid down in the sūtra इंद्र ज्येष्ठं न आ भरा त्वा सहस्रमा शतं (*iṃdra jyeṣṭhaṃ na ā bharā tvā sahasramā śataṃ*) (Ā. 7-4). O Indra, bring (आ भर (*ā bhara*), fetch, give) to us the food that is the best (ज्येष्ठं (*jyeṣṭhaṃ*), the most praiseworthy), most vigorous (ओजिष्ठं (*ojiṣṭhaṃ*), exceedingly strengthening) and filling (पपुरि (*papuri*), that which fills). O wonderful one (चित्र (*citra*), worthy of admiration), holder of the thunderbolt in your hand, O fair-jawed one (सुशिप्र (*suśipra*), having a beautiful jaw), such an Indra: the food with which you fill (प्राः (*prāḥ*)) these two visible worlds, heaven and earth (रोदसी (*rodasī*)), bring us that food: this is the construction. ⟨NOTE:62⟩
notes: ಪಪುರಿ glossed ಸೃಷ್ಟಿದಾಯಕ in the Pratipadārtha and ಪುಷ್ಟಿದಾಯಕ in the Bhāvārtha; Sāyaṇa has ಪೂರಕಂ

en: - वज्रहस्त (*vajrahasta*)—you who have a hand holding the thunderbolt
- सुशिप्र (*suśipra*)—you who have an excellent jaw
- उभे रोदसी (*ubhe rodasī*)—both heaven and earth

O Indra, attractive, with a hand holding the thunderbolt and with an excellent jaw, bring and give us such praiseworthy food, endowed with vigour and the giver of nourishment, with which you protect these two visible worlds, heaven and earth.
Indra, bring to us most excellent, most invigorating and nutritious food, wherewith, wonderful wielder of the thunderbolt, the handsome-chinned, you sustain both heaven and earth.

O shining (राजन् (*rājan*)) Indra, among the gods you are fierce (उग्रं (*ugraṃ*), of uplifted strength) and the overcomer (चर्षणीसहं (*carṣaṇīsahaṃ*)) of the carṣaṇīs, the peoples who are enemies; you we call (हूमहे (*hūmahe*), we summon) for protection. Make all the पिब्बना (*pibbanā*), the rākṣasas (so called because they utter muffled, indistinct sounds), well afflicted and hindered. O Vasu, giver of dwellings, Indra, make our enemies easy to overcome (सुषहान् (*suṣahān*)), that is, such as can be overcome with ease.
- उग्रं (*ugraṃ*)—you who have exceedingly great strength
- सुषहान् (*suṣahān*)—so that we may conquer them easily

O shining Indra, you who among the gods have exceedingly great strength and who destroy enemy armies, we call you for protection. O Indra, giver of dwellings, make all the rākṣasas completely afflicted. Help us so that we may conquer our enemies easily.
We invoke for proteetion you, royal Indra, who are mighty amongst the gods, the subduer of men; granter of dwellings, repel all evil spirits, and render our enemies easy of discomfiture.

O Indra, among the Nāhuṣī (नाहुषीषु (*nāhuṣīṣu*)): Nahuṣa is a name for man, so the word means those connected with him, the peoples (कृष्णिषु (*kṛṣṇiṣu*)); the particle आ (*ā*) expresses combination. Whatever strength (ओजः (*ojaḥ*)) and wealth (नृम्मं (*nṛmmaṃ*)) there is among them; or else whatever there is of the five peoples (क्षितीनां (*kṣitīnāṃ*)), the four classes with the Niṣādas as the fifth being the five peoples, their own nature, the shining (द्युम्नं (*dyumnaṃ*)) food: all that bring to us, give to us. And likewise bring to us all the great manly powers (पौंस्यानि (*pauṃsyāni*)).
- नृम्णं च (*nṛmṇaṃ ca*)—and wealth also there is
- पंच क्षीतीनां (*paṃca kṣītīnāṃ*)—among the five peoples beginning with the Niṣādas
- all that: आ भर (*ā bhara*)—provide for us
- विश्वानि (*viśvāni*)—and all: give all the powers

O Indra, whatever strength and wealth there is among the peoples connected with man, or whatever shining food there is among the five peoples beginning with the Niṣādas, provide all that for us. Give all the great and entire powers.
Whatever strength and opulence (exist) amongst human beings, whatever be the sustenance of the five classes of men, bring Indra to us, as well (as) all great manly energies.

O Maghavan, wealthy Indra: whatever strength there is in Tṛkṣu (तृक्षावेतत्संज्ञॆ (*tṛkṣāvetatsaṃjñè*), the king of this name); or in Druhyu, of this name, and in the people (जने (*jane*)) whatever strength there is; and in Pūru, the king of this name, whatever manly vigour (वृष्ट्यं (*vṛṣṭyaṃ*)) there is: all that give fully (सं रिरीहि (*saṃ rirīhi*), give completely) to us who are your praisers. When? When a battle is undertaken (नृसह्ये (*nṛsahye*)), one to be endured by men, by warriors. For what purpose? In the encounters (पृत्सु (*pṛtsu*), in battles), to crush (तुर्वणे (*turvaṇe*), to destroy) the enemies.
- आ जने (*ā jane*)—in the multitude of people too
- पूरौ (*pūrau*)—in the king named Pūru too
- वृष्ट्यं (*vṛṣṭyaṃ*)—manly vigour there is, तत् (*tat*)—all that

O Indra, possessor of wealth, whatever kind of vigour there is in the king named Tṛkṣu, or in the king named Druhyu, or in the king named Pūru, give all that fully to us, who are praisers, in battles in which enemies are confronted, so that we may destroy the enemies.
Whatever vigour, Maghavan, (existed) in Trikshu, in Druhyu, in Puru, bestow fully upon us in conflicts wish foes, so that we may destroy our enemies in war.

On the Cāturviṃśika day, in the niṣkevalya, the sāma-pragātha of the Vairūpa beginning इंद्र त्रिधातु (*iṃdra tridhātu*) is to be recited. It is laid down in the sūtra: इंद्र त्रिधातु शरणं त्वमिंद्र प्रशूर्तिषु (*iṃdra tridhātu śaraṇaṃ tvamiṃdra praśūrtiṣu*) (Ā. 7 3). ⟨NOTE:63⟩ O Indra, give a dwelling (शरणं (*śaraṇaṃ*), a house) that is threefold (त्रिधातु (*tridhātu*): of three kinds, of three storeys), a warder-off of three things, cold, heat and rain (त्रिवरूथं (*trivarūthaṃ*)), secure (स्वस्तिमत् (*svastimat*), free from destruction), furnished with a covering (छर्दिः (*chardiḥ*)) ⟨NOTE:64⟩; a house of such qualities: give it to those of ours who are possessed of wealth (मघवद्भ्यश्च (*maghavadbhyaśca*): magha is wealth in the form of oblations) and to me, Bharadvāja. And separate from them (यवय (*yavaya*), put apart) the flaming (दिद्युं (*didyuṃ*)) weapon sent by the enemy.
notes: the bhāṣya reads ಪ್ರಶೂರ್ತಿಷು; the Kannada ವಿಶೇಷವಿಷಯಗಳು has ಪ್ರತೂರ್ತಿಷು for the same sūtra
ಛರ್ದಿಶ್ಚದಿಷ್ಟಿಚ್ಛಾದನಯುಕ್ತಂ is damaged

en: - त्रिवरूथं (*trivarūthaṃ*)—which can protect from cold, sunshine and rain
- मघवद्ध्यः (*maghavaddhyaḥ*)—to our kinsmen, who have wealth in the form of oblations

O Indra, grant a house that is of three kinds, that can protect from cold, sunshine and rain, that is auspicious and protective, to our kinsmen, who are ready to offer oblations, and to me, Bharadvāja. Keep far from these houses the flaming weapon of the enemies, sent by the enemy, so that no harm may come to it.
Give, Indra, to the affluent, and to me also, a sheltering and prosperous dwelling, combining three elements, and defending in three ways, and keep from them the blazing (weapon of our foes).

On the day of the sacrifice called Cāturviṃśaka, when the niṣkevalya-śastra mantras are recited, this Ṛk, इंद्र त्रिधातु (*iṃdra tridhātu*), is to be recited for the sāma-pragātha mantra; this is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta-sūtra, इंद्र त्रिधातु शरणं त्वमिंद्र प्रतूर्तिषु (*iṃdra tridhātu śaraṇaṃ tvamiṃdra pratūrtiṣu*) (Ā. 7-3).

Those men who, endowed with a mind that desires the cows (गव्यता (*gavyatā*)) of their enemies, slew (आदभुः (*ādabhuḥ*), did violence to) the enemy, the foe (शायितारं (*śāyitāraṃ*)); and those who, bold (धृष्टया (*dhṛṣṭayā*)), aiming at us, strike (प्रघ्नंति (*praghnaṃti*), hurt violently): O Maghavan, wealthy Indra, sharer of songs (गिर्वणः (*girvaṇaḥ*)), at this time, from those, be the protector of our bodies (तनूपाः (*tanūpāḥ*)) and be nearest to us (अंतमः (*aṃtamaḥ*)).
- गिर्वणः (*girvaṇaḥ*)—and one to be reached by praise
- गव्यता (*gavyatā*)—desiring to obtain cows (from the enemies)
- धृष्णुया (*dhṛṣṇuyā*)—with a mind that assails enemies
- तनूपाः (*tanūpāḥ*)—as the protector of the body

O wealthy Indra, one to be reached by praise, like those men who, endowed with a mind that desires to obtain cows from the enemies, have slain the enemy, and who strike with a mind that assails enemies, be exceedingly near to us at this time.

Affluent Indra, propitiated by praise, be near to us, the defender of our persons (against those) who assail (us as) enemies, with a mind bent upon carrying off (our) cattle, or who assault us with arrogance.

O Indra, at that time be for our growth, and protect in battle whoever is our leader. Sāyaṇa supplies the answer to "at what time?": when the feathered, sharp-pointed, shining वाहा (*vāhā*) ⟨NOTE:65⟩ ones, let loose by the enemies, fall through the sky, then be for our growth. This is the construction.
notes: ವಾಹಾ in the bhāṣya, probably ಬಾಣಾ "arrows"; Kannada gloss has "arrows"

en: - दिद्यवः (*didyavaḥ*)—and shining ones, the arrows (sent by the enemies)

O Indra, when the feathered, sharp-pointed and shining arrows of the enemies, sent by the enemies, fall upon us from the sky, be to us one who brings increase (a protector). Protect our leader in battle.
Indra, be (favourable) at present to our success: protect our leader in battle when the feathered, sharp-pointed, shining shafts fall from the sky.

At the time when the brave warriors spread out their own bodies, that is, show them before the enemies for their master's victory, at that time they leave behind the pleasant dwellings that belong to their fathers, that is, that were acquired by them; they spread these out before the enemies, which means they abandon them. Then, at this time, for the body (तन्ने (*tanne*)) and for the offspring (तने (*tane*)) grant armour (छर्दिः (*chardiḥ*)), a covering that wards off weapons, in such a way that it is unknown to the enemies, that is, give it before the enemies know of it. And drive away the haters, the enemies: separate them from us.
- वितन्वते (*vitanvate*)—spread out on the battlefield (for the master's victory), at that time
- तन्ने (*tanne*)—for the protection of their bodies
- छर्दिः (*chardiḥ*)—the armour that protects their bodies
- अचित्तं (*acittaṃ*)—so that the enemies do not know it

O Indra, at the time when valiant warriors spread out their bodies on the battlefield for their master's victory, they abandon their own houses, which are pleasant, inherited from their fathers and protective. At that time give armour, unknown to the enemies, for the protection of their bodies and of their sons and others. And destroy the enemies.
When heroes rest their persons (until abandoning) the pleasant abodes of their progenitors: grant us, for ourselves and our posterity, an unsuspected defence, and scatter our enemies.

O Indra, when in a great battle (महाधने (*mahādhane*)), that is, a battle fought for the sake of great wealth that is to be won, at the time of the effort (सर्गे (*sarge*), that is, exertion) you urge our horses along an uneven, rough road, and along the crooked path that is the sky, as falcons that desire food in the form of flesh (श्रवस्यतः (*śravasyataḥ*): śravaḥ is food, flesh) fly swiftly in the sky for the sake of that food, so, when you make our horses go swiftly, then give armour for our body and our offspring: this is the connection with the preceding Ṛk. ⟨NOTE:66⟩
notes: ಸತ್ಯಸಮನೇ in the bhāṣya, where the verse has ಅಸಮನೇ; read "uneven" as in the gloss ವಿಷಮೇ

en: - श्रवस्यतः (*śravasyataḥ*)—seeking food in the form of flesh
- महाधने (*mahādhane*)—in a battle for the sake of abundant wealth
- सर्गे (*sarge*)—at the time of the effort
- असमने (*asamane*)—uneven, full of pits and mounds
- चोदयासे (*codayāse*)—you urge (to run swiftly) (then give protective armour)

O Indra, when, in a battle for the sake of abundant wealth, at the time of the effort, you urge our horses to run swiftly on a road full of pits and mounds and uneven, as falcons that seek food in the form of flesh fly swiftly on the crooked path of the sky, then give protective armour.
(At the time) when, in the effort (made) in an arduous conflict; urge our horses over an uneven road, like falcons darting upon their food through the difficult path (of the firmament).

This Ṛk is meant to establish with emphasis the meaning already stated. O Indra, if you urge horses that go swiftly (आशुया (*āśuyā*)), like streams (सिंधूनिव (*siṃdhūniva*)) flowing down a slope (प्रवणे (*pravaṇe*)); when? क्लोशमनु (*klośamanu*): क्लोश (*klośa*) is a name for fear; with regard to fear, when there is a cry (स्वनि (*svani*), in the sense of a cry). What kind are those horses? Those that are held (गृभीताः (*gṛbhītāḥ*)) at the arm-roots (बाह्वोः (*bāhvoḥ*)), that is, bound by the girth, and that, when wealth in the form of cattle (गवि (*gavi*)) is to be won, turn back again and again (वर्वृतति (*varvṛtati*)); when flesh (आमिषि (*āmiṣi*)) is to be seized they turn again and again, like birds (वयो न (*vayo na*)) such as falcons. When you urge such horses while there is a cry through fear, then give armour for those who belong to us: this is the connection. And though the ṛṣi has no occasion in war ⟨NOTE:67⟩, yet, since he is the king's chief priest, victory is prayed for the king's men, so there is no contradiction.
notes: ಯದ್ಯಪ್ಯಷೇಯೂರ್ದ್ಧೇ in the bhāṣya is damaged; read here as "though there is no occasion (for the ṛṣi) in war"; also the stray word ದಕ್ಷಿಣಃ after ಶ್ಯೇನಾದಯಃ is unclear

en: - वयो न (*vayo na*)—as falcons and other birds come running again and again
- गृभीताः (*gṛbhītāḥ*)—which are bound with a girth
- आ वर्वृतति (*ā varvṛtati*)—which come again and again
- यदि (*yadi*)—when you urge (then give armour for war)

O Indra, those horses which are bound with a girth at the arm-roots, and which come back again and again for the sake of cattle, as falcons and other birds come running again and again to obtain flesh, even though those horses are neighing through fear, when you urge them to run very swiftly, like rivers flowing rapidly in low-lying places, then give armour for war.

Rushing rapidly like rivers in their downward course, and although neighing loudly through terror, they yet, tight-girthed, return repeatedly (to the conflict) for cattle, like birds darting on their prey.

This pressed Soma is indeed sweet to the taste (स्वादुः (*svāduḥ*)). It is also honeyed (मधुमान् (*madhumān*)), that is, full of sweetness. This Soma is likewise keen (तीव्रः (*tīvraḥ*)): in producing intoxication it is sharp. And it is full of juice (रसवान् (*rasavān*)), that is, full of essence. By these four statements the surpassing sweetness of Soma is set forth. Further, no one in battles can overcome Indra, who has drunk (पपिवांसं (*papivāṃsaṃ*)) this Soma. The word नु (*nu*) is a mere filler.
- तीव्रः किल (*tīvraḥ kila*)—has a sharpness that causes intoxication
- न सहते नु (*na sahate nu*)—can withstand and defeat

This pressed Soma is certainly savoury. It is endowed with sweetness and full of juice, and moreover has a sharpness that causes intoxication. No one in battles can withstand and defeat Indra who drinks this Soma juice.
Savoury indeed is this (Soma); sweet is it, sharp, and full of flavour: no one is able to encounter Indra in battles after he has been quaffing this (beverage).

Here, in this sacrifice, this Soma, tasted, that is, drunk, has become most intoxicating, intoxicating to the highest degree. By drinking this Soma Indra became exhilarated at the time of the slaying of Vṛtra. This Soma also destroyed the many strengths (च्यौत्ना (*cyautnā*)) of the asura Śambara. Likewise, the Soma destroyed ninety-nine (नवतिं नव च (*navatiṃ nava ca*)) of the demons' strongholds, built-up and accumulated ones (देहो (*deho*)), or else their bodies. This is connected with अयं सोमः (*ayaṃ somaḥ*), "this Soma", of the first line.
- वृत्रहत्ये (*vṛtrahatye*)—at the time of slaying Vṛtra
- नवतिं नव च (*navatiṃ nava ca*)—ninety-nine in number

By drinking which Soma Indra obtained exhilaration at the time of slaying the asura Vṛtra, which Soma became the means of killing the numerous armies of the asura Śambara, and by drinking which he slew the ninety-nine firm cities of the asuras, this Soma is, in this sacrifice, savoury and intoxicating.

This savoury Soma, drunk on this occasion, has been most exhilarating : dy drinking of it Indra, has been elevated to the slaying of Vritra, and it has destroyed the numerous hosts of Sambara and the ninety-nine cities.

This Soma, when drunk, brings forth, that is, makes manifest, my speech (वाचं (*vācaṃ*)). This same Soma brings forth and makes manifest the desired (उशतीं (*uśatīṃ*)), lovely intelligence (मनीषां (*manīṣāṃ*)). And this wise Soma created the six wide ones ⟨NOTE:73⟩, which are set forth as heaven and earth, day and night, the waters and the plants. Than these wide ones, far away, in a distant place, there is no other being or world whatever; rather, all beings exist in these very ones. Such wide ones he created.
notes: the words ಸಳುರ್ವಿಃ ಷಣ್ಮೋರ್ವೀರಂಹಸಸ್ಪಾಂತು ದ್ಯೌಷ್ಟ in the bhāṣya are damaged

en: - षट्.उर्विः (*ṣaṭ.urviḥ*)—six worlds beginning with the heavenly world

This Soma juice, when drunk, makes my speech manifest. This same Soma makes the attractive intelligence grow sharp. This wise Soma king created the six principles, the heavenly world, the earth, day, night, waters and plants, beyond which there is no other world.
This beverage inspires my speech; this develops the desired intelligence: this sagacious (Soma) has created the six vast conditions, from which no creature is distinct.

This is that Soma who made the extent (वरिमाणं (*varimāṇaṃ*)), the wideness and expansion, of the earth. Likewise this Soma made the compactness (वर्ष्णाणं (*varṣṇāṇaṃ*)), the firmness, of the heaven. ⟨NOTE:74⟩ This Soma also holds the juice, the ambrosia (पीयूषं (*pīyūṣaṃ*)), in the three ⟨NOTE:75⟩, in these excellent ones (प्रवत्सु (*pravatsu*)). And he holds up the wide firmament. He quotes another mantra: त्वमिमा ओषधीः सोम विश्वास्त्वमपो अजनयस्त्वं गाः । त्वमा ततंथोर्वंतरिक्षं (*tvamimā oṣadhīḥ soma viśvāstvamapo ajanayastvaṃ gāḥ | tvamā tataṃthorvaṃtarikṣaṃ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-91-22) **GLOSS** ⟨NOTE:76⟩
notes: ಅಯಂ ಸೋಮ॥ ಸ ಹಿ ಭವತಿ in the bhāṣya is damaged
ತಿ ಸೃಷ್ಟೋಷಧೀಷ್ಟಪ್ಪು ಗೋಷು in the bhāṣya is damaged; the Kannada gloss has plants, waters and cows
abbreviation ಋಗ್ವೇ. printed

en: - आयं सोमः (*āyaṃ somaḥ*)—is this Soma king
- पीयूषं (*pīyūṣaṃ*)—the juice of the nature of ambrosia

He who made the earth exceedingly wide, he who made the heavenly world stand firm, is this Soma king. This same Soma has filled the most excellent plants, waters and cows with the juice of the nature of ambrosia. And he has upheld the wide firmament.
This it is which has formed the earth, the compactness of the heaven : this soma has deposited the ambrosia in its three principal (receptacles). and has upheld the spacious firmament.

This Soma obtains (विदत् (*vidat*)), that is, causes to be obtained, the wonderfully visible (चित्रदृशीकं (*citradṛśīkaṃ*)), or marvellously beautiful, solar light (अर्णः (*arṇaḥ*)), the impeller of all. At what time? At the front, at the head, of the dawns (उषसां (*uṣasāṃ*)) whose seat is the pure firmament; that is, at the time of dawn. And this great (महान् (*mahān*)), grown Soma has propped up (उदस्तभ्नात् (*udastabhnāt*)) the heavenly world with a great, most massive prop, namely the firmament that stands in the middle: he set it upright, and made the firmament its support so that it does not fall downward. What kind of Soma? A bull (वृषभः (*vṛṣabhaḥ*)), the producer of rain; for by the oblation of Soma rain is produced. He is accompanied by the Maruts (मरुत्वान् (*marutvān*)).
- शुक्रसद्मनां (*śukrasadmanāṃ*)—those whose dwelling is the shining firmament
- अनीके (*anīke*)—at the time of their appearing
- स्कंभनेन (*skaṃbhanena*)—firmament that is like a supporting pillar
- उदस्तभ्नात् (*udastabhnāt*)—has established and made to stand

At the time of the appearing of the dawns, whose dwelling is the shining firmament, this Soma king makes manifest the most attractively visible light of the sun. This Soma king, the producer of rain, accompanied by the Maruts, and great-souled, has established and made to stand the heavenly world with the help of the firmament, which is like a most firm supporting pillar.

This makes known the wonderfully beautiful and inspiring (solar radiance) at the appearance of the dawns, whose dwelling is the firmament : this mighty (Soma) has sustained the heaven with a powerful support, the sender of rain, the leader of the winds.

O hero, O Indra, you who slay the Vṛtras, the enemies who obstruct, when a battle for wealth has come about, drink boldly (धृषत् (*dhṛṣat*)), that is, in such a way that you become bold, the Soma standing in the Droṇa-kalaśa (कलशे (*kalaśe*)). Also pour in (आ वृषस्व (*ā vṛṣasva*)), that is, fill your belly with Soma at the midday pressing; for the midday pressing belongs wholly to Indra. And, as the abode of riches (रयिस्थानः (*rayisthānaḥ*)), place riches in us.
- समरे (*samare*)—in order to take part in the battle
- धृषत् (*dhṛṣat*)—so that strength and courage are filled
- माध्यंदिने सवने (*mādhyaṃdine savane*)—also at the time of the midday pressing
- आ वृषस्व (*ā vṛṣasva*)—fill the belly fully with Soma
- रयिस्थानः (*rayisthānaḥ*)—you, the place of origin of riches

O valiant Indra, you, the slayer of Vṛtra, drink the Soma that is in the Droṇa-kalaśa, so that you are filled with strength and courage, in order to take part in the battle that is fought for riches. At the time of the midday pressing also fill your belly fully with Soma. You, the place of origin of riches, fill us fully with riches.

Hero, Indra, you are the slayer of foes in contests for (the acquirement of) treasures, drink boldly from the pitcher : drink copiously at the noon-day rite : receptacle of riches, bestow riches upon us.

O Indra, look upon us (प्र पश्य (*pra paśya*)) like one who goes in front (पुरएतेव (*puraeteva*)). ⟨NOTE:77⟩ As a guardian of the road, going in front himself, sees the travellers who follow and are to be protected, so look upon us: this is the meaning. Likewise lead us (प्र णय (*pra ṇaya*)) towards the best, most excellent wealth (वस्यः (*vasyaḥ*)), facing us, to an excess. Be a good ferrier (सुपारः (*supāraḥ*)), one who takes us across sorrows. Make us pass beyond (अतिपारयः (*atipārayaḥ*)) the enemies ⟨NOTE:78⟩. Be for us a good leader (सुनीतिः (*sunītiḥ*)), and also a leader of the desirable (वामानां (*vāmānāṃ*)), enjoyable riches (वामनीतिः (*vāmanītiḥ*)). Or else: be for our sake the conveyer to the best.
notes: ಪ್ರಕರ್ಷೇಣೇಕಸ್ಯ in the bhāṣya, perhaps a damaged form of "look attentively"
ಸ್ತೋತ್ಥನತಿಪಾರಯಃ in the bhāṣya, damaged

en: - पुर एतेव (*pura eteva*)—like one who goes right in front of us
- सुपारः (*supāraḥ*)—as one who brings to an end from sorrow
- अतिपारयः (*atipārayaḥ*)—free from the grip of the enemies
- सुनीतिः (*sunītiḥ*)—as an excellent guide for us
- वामनीतिः (*vāmanītiḥ*)—be also one who supplies attractive wealth

O Indra, be right in front of us and look upon us fully. Supply us with excellent wealth. Bring us to the end of sorrow. Free us from the grip of the enemies. Be for us an excellent guide and also one who supplies attractive wealth.

Like one who goes before us, Indra, (on the road), look out, bring before us infinite wealth ; be our conductor beyond the bounds (of want) convey us safely over (peril); be our careful guide, our guide to desirable (affluence).

In the animal sacrifice to Indra this Ṛk, उरुं नः (*uruṃ naḥ*), is the yājyā for the omentum (vapā); and it is prescribed in the sūtra: उरुं नो लोकमनु नेषि विद्वान् प्र ससाहिषे पुरुहूत शत्रून् (*uruṃ no lokamanu neṣi vidvān pra sasāhiṣe puruhūta śatrūn*) (Ā. 3-7). The assistants of the Hotṛ also mutter it when they approach the sadas, as the sūtra says: उरुं नो लोकमनु नेषि विद्वानिति जपंतः (*uruṃ no lokamanu neṣi vidvāniti japaṃtaḥ*) (Ā. 5-3). On the Cāturviṃśika day, and on the second and following days in the ahargaṇas, at the midday pressing it is the opening verse (ārambhaṇīyā) of the Acchāvāka, as the sūtra says: उरुं नो लोकमनु नेषि विद्वानिति कद्वद्भ्य आरंभणीयाः (*uruṃ no lokamanu neṣi vidvāniti kadvadbhya āraṃbhaṇīyāḥ*) (Ā. 7-4). O Indra, you who know, lead us (अनु नेषि (*anu neṣi*)), cause us to reach, the wide (उरुं (*uruṃ*)) world (लोकं (*lokaṃ*)), the place called heaven; and, with well-being (स्वस्ति (*svasti*)), lead us to light that is full of happiness (स्वर्वत् (*svarvat*)) and free from fear. O Indra, your two arms, lovely (ऋष्वा (*ṛṣvā*)) to behold and great (बृहंता (*bṛhaṃtā*)), belonging to you who are stout (स्थविरस्य (*sthavirasya*)), that is, big and old, as protectors (शरणा (*śaraṇā*)): may we resort to, serve, those arms of yours (उपस्थेयाम (*upastheyāma*)).
- स्वस्ति (*svasti*)—so that well-being comes to us
- स्थविरस्य (*sthavirasya*)—of you who are of firm body
- शरणा (*śaraṇā*)—so that they are protectors for us
- उपस्थेयाम (*upastheyāma*)—may we take refuge in them and be happy

O Indra, you who know everything, lead us and bring us, so that well-being comes to us, to a place that is full of happiness, free from fear, peaceful and wide. O Indra, may we take refuge in your attractive and long arms, you who are of firm body, so that they are protectors for us, and be happy.

Do you, Indra, who are wise, conduct us to the spacious world (of heaven), to a blessed state of happiness, light, and safety : may we recline in the graceful, protecting, and mighty arms of you the ancient one.

Although there is a difference of opinion on the question whether the gods have hands, feet and other limbs as human beings have, it is seen in the Ṛgveda that the seers praised Indra and the other gods, thinking of them as having hands, feet and other limbs. In this matter Yāska has given the explanation: अथाकारचिंतनं देवतानां । पुरुषविधाः स्युरित्येकं चेतनावद्वद्धि स्तुतयो भवंति । तथाभिधानानि । अथापि पौरुषविधिकैरंगैः संस्तूयंते । ऋष्वात इंद्र स्थविरस्य बाहू । यत्संगृभ्णा मघवन् काशिरित्ते ॥ (*athākāraciṃtanaṃ devatānāṃ | puruṣavidhāḥ syurityekaṃ cetanāvadvaddhi stutayo bhavaṃti | tathābhidhānāni | athāpi pauruṣavidhikairaṃgaiḥ saṃstūyaṃte | ṛṣvāta iṃdra sthavirasya bāhū | yatsaṃgṛbhṇā maghavan kāśiritte ‖*) (Ni. 7-6). Now let us examine the form, shape and so on of the gods. It is the opinion of some that the gods have hands and other limbs, as men have. Thinking that, as men have consciousness, so the gods also have consciousness, intelligence and so on, and since the gods also have limbs such as hands, and a form, as men have, they are thought of as endowed with consciousness,

and they are praised accordingly. For this very reason it is the custom, when describing Indra and the other gods, to describe their hands and so on. In the third pāda of the present Ṛk, ऋष्वात इंद्र स्थविरस्य बाहू (*ṛṣvāta iṃdra sthavirasya bāhū*), there is a description of the arms of Indra. Likewise the authors of the Nirukta have cited, as one in which also there is a description of the limbs of Indra, the Ṛk: उताभये पुरुहूत श्रवोभिरेको दृळ्मवदो वृत्रहा सन् । इमे चिदिंद्र रोदसी अपारे यत्संगृभ्णा मघवन् काशिरित्ते ॥ (*utābhaye puruhūta śravobhireko dṛḷmavado vṛtrahā san | ime cidiṃdra rodasī apāre yatsaṃgṛbhṇā maghavan kāśiritte ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-30-5) **GLOSS**

There are many descriptions saying that the gods have, besides the forms of men and the like, also union with various objects, as men have: अथापि पौरुषविधिकैर्द्रव्यसंयोगैः (*athāpi pauruṣavidhikairdravyasaṃyogaiḥ*) (Ni. 7-6). In this matter, after giving the example of the Ṛk आ द्वाभ्यां हरिभ्यामिंद्र याह्या चतुर्भिरा षड्भिर्हूयमानः । आष्टाभिर्दशभिः सोमपेयमयं सुतः सुमख मा मृधस्कः । (*ā dvābhyāṃ haribhyāmiṃdra yāhyā caturbhirā ṣaḍbhirhūyamānaḥ | āṣṭābhirdaśabhiḥ somapeyamayaṃ sutaḥ sumakha mā mṛdhaskaḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-18-4), it is clearly explained in this Ṛk that, as men have cows, horses and the like, so Indra and the other gods also have them. "O Indra, come to our sacrifice, seated in your chariot, together with your two horses named Hari; or else come here to drink Soma together with four, six, eight or ten horses": since this is said, the idea becomes evident that, as in worldly dealings men have possessions, so the gods also have horses and the like. And further: अपाः सोममस्तमिंद्र प्र याहि कल्याणीर्जाया सुरणं गृहे ते । यत्रा रथस्य बृहतो निधानं विमोचनं वाजिनो दक्षिणावत् ॥ (*apāḥ somamastamiṃdra pra yāhi kalyāṇīrjāyā suraṇaṃ gṛhe te | yatrā rathasya bṛhato nidhānaṃ vimocanaṃ vājino dakṣiṇāvat ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-53-6). In this Ṛk there is a mention of the fact that, as men have, so Indra also has at home a wife, a chariot and horses.
Further, they have defended, by giving some examples, the view that the gods also have actions like the actions of men: अथापि पौरुषविधिकैः कर्मभिः (*athāpi pauruṣavidhikaiḥ karmabhiḥ*) (Ni. 7-6).

इदं हविर्मघवन् तुभ्यं रातं प्रति सम्राळहृणानो गृभाय । तुभ्यं सुतो मघवन् तुभ्यं पक्वोत्थींद्र पिब च प्रस्थितस्य ॥ (*idaṃ havirmaghavan tubhyaṃ rātaṃ prati samrāḷahṛṇāno gṛbhāya | tubhyaṃ suto maghavan tubhyaṃ pakvotthīṃdra piba ca prasthitasya ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-16-7). आश्रुत्कर्ण श्रुधी हवं नू चिद्दधिष्ट मे गिरः । इंद्र स्तोममिमं मम कृष्णा युजश्चिदंतरं ॥ (*āśrutkarṇa śrudhī havaṃ nū ciddadhiṣṭa me giraḥ | iṃdra stomamimaṃ mama kṛṣṇā yujaścidaṃtaraṃ ‖*). These Ṛks have been given as examples. In the first Ṛk it is said that an oblation and Soma have been offered for Indra, and it is prayed that Indra should drink it. In the second Ṛk there is a prayer that he should hear our invocation and our hymn. That is, actions fitting to men, such as eating the oblation as men do, drinking the Soma juice, and listening to and hearing the invocation and the hymn, are ascribed also to Indra and the other gods in praising them. In this way it is the contention of some that, like men, the gods also have form, hands and other limbs, and actions such as eating. Others hold that the gods have no form and so on as men have, that their actions are also different from the actions that men perform, and that the gods are described in that way, by exaggeration, in order to describe their greatness: अपुरुषविधाः स्युरित्यपरं (*apuruṣavidhāḥ syurityaparaṃ*) (Ni. 7-7).

Still others hold that the gods have no form, shape, actions and the like as men have, and that their distinguishing marks are of another kind. How? अपि तु यद्दृश्यतेऽपुरुषविधं तद्यथाग्निर्वायुरादित्यः पृथिवी चंद्रमा इति ॥ (*api tu yaddṛśyate 'puruṣavidhaṃ tadyathāgnirvāyurādityaḥ pṛthivī caṃdramā iti ‖*) (Ni. 7-7). Although the forms and actions of some gods appear as those of men, they are not so. Although the forms and actions of such gods as Agni, Vāyu, Āditya, Pṛthivī and Candramā appear like the actions of men, their manner is different. There is a particular difference between those actions and the actions of men.

यथो एतच्चेतनावद्वद्धि स्तुतयो भवंतीत्यचेतनान्यप्येपं स्तूयंते यथाक्षप्रभृतीनोषधिपर्यंतानि ॥ (*yatho etaccetanāvadvaddhi stutayo bhavaṃtītyacetanānyapyepaṃ stūyaṃte yathākṣaprabhṛtīnoṣadhiparyaṃtāni ‖*) (Ni. 7-7). That is, when gods such as Agni are praised, they are praised as though they had consciousness. When gambling, people address the dice; though the dice are devoid of consciousness, they address them as living beings with consciousness. They address plants as well, that is, shrubs, trees and creepers, thinking of them as having consciousness.

यथो एतत्पौरुषविधिकैरंगैः संस्तूयंत इत्यचेतनेष्वप्येतद्भवत्यभिक्रदंति हरितेभिरासभिरिति ग्रावस्तुतिः ॥ (*yatho etatpauruṣavidhikairaṃgaiḥ saṃstūyaṃta ityacetaneṣvapyetadbhavatyabhikradaṃti haritebhirāsabhiriti grāvastutiḥ ‖*) (Ni. 7-7). In the same way, things without consciousness are also praised, as though they had limbs belonging to men. Plants and the stones that crush Soma are without consciousness. Yet the sound that arises when the Soma plants are crushed with stones is described by saying that those stones cry out with their green mouths. Since stones are without consciousness, they have no mouths as living beings have. Yet the seer has described in a figurative way the sound that is made when a plant is placed on a stone and crushed, as the stones making it with their own mouths. When Soma plants are crushed, the green colour of those plants clings to the stones; to suggest that the mouths of the stones are of green colour, a description with exaggeration has been made, that the mouths of the stones are of green colour.

यथो एतत्पौरुषविधिकैर्द्रव्यसंयोगैरित्येतदपि तादृशमेव । सुखं रथं युयुजे सिंधुरश्विनं इति नदीस्तुतिः ॥ (*yatho etatpauruṣavidhikairdravyasaṃyogairityetadapi tādṛśameva | sukhaṃ rathaṃ yuyuje siṃdhuraśvinaṃ iti nadīstutiḥ ‖*) (Ni. 7-7). In the matter of things without consciousness also having union with objects, as men have: as in sentences such as "the river (Sindhu) yoked her horses to a pleasant chariot", the river, being a thing without consciousness, has no chariot. Yet, in praising the river, the seer has praised it by ascribing to the river, as to men, union with objects (the possession of property).

यथो एतत्पौरुषविधिकैः कर्मभिरित्येतदपि तादृशमेव । होतुश्चित्पूर्वे हविरद्यमाशत इति ग्रावस्तु तिरेव ॥ (*yatho etatpauruṣavidhikaiḥ karmabhirityetadapi tādṛśameva | hotuścitpūrve haviradyamāśata iti grāvastu tireva ‖*) (Ni. 7-7). In the matter of actions also, agency in action has been ascribed, as to men, to things without consciousness such as stones, and they have been praised. When the Soma plant is crushed with a stone, it is natural that the juice that comes out of the plant touches the stone. This is what the seer has described by saying that the stones, the means of pressing the Soma, taste the Soma juice before the sacrificers such as the Hotṛ. A stone has no mouth, and it has no capacity to taste. Yet, since the juice that comes out when the plant is crushed with the stone touches the stone, the description that the stone tastes the Soma juice before everyone is made with exaggeration and in a figurative way. That stones, being without consciousness, have neither a mouth nor the capacity to taste is a matter established by the experience of all.

अपि वा पुरुषविधानामेव सतां कर्मात्मन एते स्युर्यथा यज्ञो यजमानस्य । एष चाख्यानसमयः ॥ (*api vā puruṣavidhānāmeva satāṃ karmātmana ete syuryathā yajño yajamānasya | eṣa cākhyānasamayaḥ ‖*) (Ni. 7-7) **GLOSS**
